canvas.title: Canvas
canvas.intro: A skill that brings scenarios, annotations, a zoomable screen board, and developer inspection into one review experience.
canvas.problem: A prototype is easy to share and hard to review. A link does not tell someone which clicks matter, which rules are hidden, or how to reach a particular state. A linear walkthrough only explains one path. I built Canvas to make the cases, the board, and the developer view part of the prototype itself.
canvas.how: Scenarios put a reviewer into a useful case with one click. Modes describe states such as role, permission, or locale, with an explicit way in and out. Numbered pins explain rules beside the UI. Deep links open the same case for the next reviewer. The board uses static snapshots instead of running every screen at once, and Inspect turns an element into a build prompt.
canvas.closing: One place to review the whole experience.
canvas.end: Canvas brings together the earlier walkthrough, Prototype Canvas, and Inspect tools. The runtime is copied into prototypes and checked against a hash manifest. The public demonstration below uses this portfolio, not an internal product. Pinned notes and viewer comments remain directions for the original tool.
canvas.demoCopy: Switch real portfolio scenarios, open a board of captured pages, or inspect actual elements and copy a build prompt.

lumina.title: Lumina
lumina.tag: From a feature to a shared understanding.
lumina.intro: A design enablement agent that turns Figma designs or running prototypes into documents, context packets, and presentation decks.
lumina.problem: When a feature is designed, other teams still need to explain it. Marketing, training, presenters, and technical writers were asking designers for walkthroughs or interpreting screenshots without context. I built Lumina to give those teams a starting point they could read, present, and ask questions about.
lumina.how: A designer points Lumina at a Figma section, a document folder, or a running prototype. It writes a structured screen-by-screen document, combines design and product context into a packet, and creates a deck on the brand template. Ask commands answer from those sources. For prototypes, a links file keeps the live QA screens and states within reach.
lumina.closing: The design becomes useful beyond design.
lumina.end: Lumina supports documents, packets, decks, source-grounded questions, frame discovery, and frame exports. This public demo assembles a small enablement packet about the portfolio itself. It demonstrates the output structure with sample content; it does not run the work agent or connect to internal systems.
lumina.demo: One website. Different ways to explain it.
lumina.demoCopy: Choose an output. Every example describes this portfolio, with the source and intended audience kept visible.

margo.title: Margo
margo.tag: Put the behavior back beside the design.
margo.intro: An agent that reads a coded prototype and places interaction notes beside the corresponding Figma mockups.
margo.problem: A prototype shows how something behaves. A mockup shows how it looks. The rules between the two were getting lost or being typed out by hand. I built Margo to turn the prototype logic into short notes, placed beside the screen where someone needs them.
margo.how: Margo reads the prototype, writes interaction notes, and places them as reusable annotation cards next to the right artboards. When the source is inaccessible, it provides an extraction prompt to run inside that environment. Optional companions capture flow states with notes and flag design-system components that are not yet implemented.
margo.end: The name comes from marginalia: notes in the margins. Margo packages the core annotation workflow and optional flow-screenshot and component-gap checks as skills. This diagram uses portfolio screens and illustrative notes. It is not a live Figma file, and the sample gap is not an audit finding about this website.
margo.demo: A handoff you can actually read.
margo.demoCopy: Toggle the notes, select a card, and see the behavior beside its screen. This is an interactive handoff diagram using the portfolio.

mosquito.title: Mosquito
mosquito.tag: Catch the drift before it ships.
mosquito.intro: A design-system QA agent that audits code against the team’s system, from tokens and spacing to focus states and accessibility.
mosquito.problem: Design-system drift often appears late: a near-match color, an off-scale spacing value, a missing focus ring. I built Mosquito to bring those checks closer to the code, while there is still time to fix them.
mosquito.how: Mosquito accepts a source path or running localhost URL. For a URL, it inspects rendered HTML and styles, then finds the matching source. It checks tokens, colors, states, focus rings, accessibility patterns, typography, and spacing. Focused accessibility, spacing, and visual modes report findings with file and line references.
mosquito.end: The original tool checks the Absorb design system and includes documentation generation and per-component QA specifications. This public demo uses this portfolio’s tokens and radii instead. The snippet and findings are illustrative, not a live repository audit or a claim about the original design system.
mosquito.demo: A small example of useful QA.
mosquito.demoCopy: Run an illustrative check, inspect the findings, then apply the fixes to see the difference. The rules here belong to this portfolio.
